title_content.content: CERTIFY OR REFUSE: A CROSS-MODEL MAP FOR SELECTIVE RISK CONTROL WITH COVERAGE FLOORS UNDER COVARIATE SHIFT

item_content.content: Jiamiao Liu Dewen Qiao Yu Zhang Xuetao Chen* Department of Information, Xinqiao Hospital
Army Medical University (Third Military Medical University) Chongqing 400037, China xuetao@tmmu.edu.cn

paragraph_content.content: Selective predictors with certified risk attain whatever coverage they attain; operators, however, impose an automation floor: answer at least a β-fraction of shifted target traffic while keeping at most an α-fraction of returned answers wrong. Under bounded-ratio covariate shift, we prove the Floor Certification Map: once that hard coverage floor β must be certified alongside the selectionconditioned risk level α, certification acquires a feasibility frontier and a two-resource samplecomplexity map, additive up to constants: risk paid in labeled source samples, the floor in unlabeled target samples. Bounded-ratio shift alone buys the frontier; the two-resource rates are local, holding under a regular frontier margin and at slack below the local-regime threshold, with the upper bounds on a pre-registered nested-threshold lattice meeting a lattice margin condition and the lower bound on a compatible lattice constructed per slack. The displayed resource split is the operational route, since under oracle weights the floor additionally admits a labeled-source estimate that only weakens the requirement. We give the map as three model-tagged results: a lower bound (Model-B), a matching oracle-weight upper bound (Model-A), and an implementable upper bound (Model-B<sup>′</sup>), valid under a pre-registered exact stratified-shift model with nuisance cost priced explicitly. The match is across these three models rather than a single-model minimax theorem, and necessarily so: over the full bounded-ratio class no unknown-weight procedure matches at any sample size (Model-B is inconsistent, witnessed at

. So no single-model law holds over that class, and the cross-model map is the correct object, not a substitute for one. The nuisance’s necessity is only partially settled. The upper bound’s variance term is an accepted-region quantity bounded by a localized second moment, and the lower-bound hard slices localize to the same region, with no global effective-sample-size (ESS) term appearing on either side, though a fixed-ESS separation theorem is left open; both lower-bound axes vanish as

so the floor creates the map. Empirically, the registered bite family diverges with log–log slope −2.002 (within its pre-registered band); a 1,024-cell audit records 0 violations where the formal certificates fire; and a single-corpus SQuAD→NewsQA feasibility audit returns honest refusal.
Keywords: selective risk control, covariate shift, conformal risk control, distribution-free certification, sample complexity lower bounds

An operator deploying a selective question-answering system commits to answering automatically at least a β-fraction of target traffic, with at most an α-fraction of the automatically returned answers wrong. Given n labeled samples from the calibration distribution and m unlabeled queries from the shifted target, when can this double promise be certified, and when is the only honest output a refusal?

paragraph_content.content: Selection-conditioned risk control exists in several forms (linear-expectation reformulation [Wang et al., 2025b], weighted e-values [Bai and Jin, 2026], cascaded calibration [Jia et al., 2026]), built on selective classification [Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017], risk control as multiple testing [Angelopoulos et al., 2021], and weighted conformal prediction [Tibshirani et al., 2019]; heuristic confidence deferral provably degrades under shift [Jitkrittum et al., 2023]. Yet all of these certify the risk of whatever coverage they attain. The classical reject-option line does characterize a risk–coverage frontier, but only the population frontier under a guaranteed-coverage (bounded-abstention) objective [Franc et al., 2023]. What is missing is the finite-sample object: no prior work proves lower bounds indexed by a coverage floor under covariate shift, nor maps what that floor costs in labeled versus unlabeled data; the nearest distribution-free lower-bound theory [Aldirawi et al., 2026] is floor-free: one axis, no coverage-floor parameter anywhere. Concretely, a risk-only certificate can be vacuously safe by abstaining on nearly all queries; it bounds the error of the few answers it does return while never guaranteeing that the operator’s β-fraction of target traffic is automated at all; the floor is exactly the promise these certificates cannot make. This paper shows the floor changes the statistical problem. We prove the Floor Certification Map: a hard coverage floor under covariate shift splits certification cost into a labeled-source risk axis and an unlabeled-target floor axis. We also run a single-corpus SQuAD→NewsQA feasibility audit of the certificate’s honest refusal. Certifying means selecting one policy λ from a pre-fixed lattice of thresholds and returning the certificate
or else issuing an honest refusal ⊥ when no policy can be certified. The frontier
is the largest coverage certifiable at risk α.

We delimit our claim sharply against the strongest neighbors. What is new is the covariate-shift theory the floor creates, the β-indexed lower bounds, the two-resource map, the localized complexity, and the budgeted-nuisance analysis, none of which these lines produce: no lower bound indexed by a coverage floor, no β-indexed matching rates, no frontier and feasibility theory. The certificate’s validity half is not new, and we say so concretely: a floor-augmented e-value construction in the spirit of SCoRE [Bai and Jin, 2026], or BalanceRAG-like cascaded-calibration machinery [Jia et al., 2026], recovers a U1-style certificate, and in the i.i.d. setting a joint finite-sample certificate for selection-conditioned risk and an acceptance floor is already available [Yu and Liu, 2026]; we therefore claim no novelty for the floor certificate itself, only for the four items above. Consistent with this scoping, our SCoRE-inspired betting arm (a risk-test ablation inside
construction, not a source-faithful SCoRE implementation) is valid and even modestly more powerful than Algorithm 1 in observed certification frequency (0 violations, certify-frequency

s across all 1,024 audited cells at the same powered-cell count; §5.2, Appendix G): a finite-sample power advantage for the certificate is neither claimed nor needed. A separate i.i.d. selective conformal risk-control line combines confident-sample selection with conformal risk control (CRC) under exchangeability/PAC-style guarantees [Xu et al., 2025b]; it does not address bounded-ratio covariate shift, β-indexed lower bounds, or the labeled-source/unlabeled-target floor-certification map studied here. Selection-conditioned and ratio risk control. The accepted-answer ratio risk E[LS]/E[S] is now an active neighborhood (linear-expectation reformulation [Wang et al., 2025b], weighted e-values for general selective risks [Bai and Jin, 2026], cascaded lattice calibration [Jia et al., 2026], risk-aware routing with abstention [Hao et al., 2026]), with the lineage running back to selective classification and classification with a reject option [Chow, 1970, El-Yaniv and Wiener, 2010, Bartlett and Wegkamp, 2008, Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017, Franc et al., 2023] and conformal selection, whose false discovery rate is itself a selected-set ratio [Jin and Candès, 2023a,b]. These certify whatever coverage the policy attains rather than a certified floor under shift; the reject-option formulations [Franc et al., 2023] do target a guaranteed-coverage (bounded-abstention) objective, but characterize the population optimum, without finite-sample floor-indexed certificates or rates under covariate shift.

Risk control under covariate shift. Importance weighting under covariate shift [Shimodaira, 2000] and weighted conformal prediction, a covariate-shift extension of conformal prediction [Vovk et al., 2022], introduced the density-ratio reweighting we build on [Tibshirani et al., 2019], extended beyond exchangeability [Barber et al., 2023] and to (high-probability) risk control under shift [Zecchin et al., 2025, Almeida et al., 2025], with direct ratio estimators and doubly robust, debiased, clipped, fine-grained, and kernel-matched weights making estimation practical [Kanamori et al., 2009, Yang et al., 2024, Kato et al., 2023, Wang and Goel, 2026, Laghuvarapu et al., 2026, Ai and Ren, 2024]. This family certifies marginal risk or coverage, never the selected-set ratio with a floor, with global ESS-type complexity rather than our localized functional.

Lower bounds and feasibility for distribution-free certification. A lower-bound culture exists: matching minimax bounds for non-monotone conformal risk control [Aldirawi et al., 2026], tight abstention bounds under adversarial injections [Edelman and Goel, 2026], overlap obstructions [D’Amour et al., 2021], prediction sets adaptive to unknown shift [Qiu et al., 2023], and tolerant learning with abstention [Goel et al., 2024]. All are floor-free: no β in any rate, hence no frontier, no two-resource (n, m) map. Our Claim-1 constructions live at bounded ratio, so they are not overlap results in disguise (Appendix B).

Learnability and estimability under arbitrary covariate shift. Closest in spirit to our impossibility leg are two lines asking when shift is tractable at all: reject-to-learn, where abstaining on unlabeled target points recovers efficient learnability under arbitrary covariate shift through a reliable-learner oracle [Kalai and Kanade, 2021]; and covariate-shifted mean estimation, which recovers E [f] for an unknown bounded f from labeled source and unlabeled target samples under structural conditions [Adil and Błasiok, 2026]. Our Model-B inconsistency (Theorem 6) is the certification analogue of the estimability boundary these navigate: over the unrestricted bounded-ratio class no (n, m)-uniform certificate exists, and the pre-registered K-cell Model-B<sup>′</sup> is the structural restriction that restores it, paralleling the structure those works impose. Neither subsumes floor-indexed certification (no coverage floor, no β-indexed rate, no risk–coverage frontier), but they locate why the floor is hard under shift.

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and cascade deployment. Certified RAG generation risk [Kang et al., 2024], conformal retrieval-augmented question answering [Li et al., 2024], conformal factuality [Mohri and Hashimoto, 2024], conformal abstention [Abbasi-Yadkori et al., 2024], and chance-constrained hallucination control [Mohandas, 2026] supply the loss substrate and baselines for our real-workload audit; the proof that confidence-based deferral fails under shift [Jitkrittum et al., 2023], together with selective question answering under domain shift via a learned calibrator [Kamath et al., 2020], supplies its motivation; none certify a coverage floor or price what the floor costs.

What is new here, exactly. The novelty is not the coverage floor as a population object (the reject-option line already studies guaranteed-coverage selective risk [Franc et al., 2023]) but the finite-sample theory the floor creates under covariate shift: β-indexed lower bounds, the two-resource (labeled/unlabeled) map, the localized accepted-region complexity, and the B<sup>′</sup> budgeted-nuisance analysis, not weighted testing, ratio linearization, or cascaded-RAG calibration, which we inherit and credit [Bates et al., 2021, Angelopoulos et al., 2021, 2024, Laufer-Goldshtein et al., 2023, Jia et al., 2026, Wang et al., 2025b, Tsybakov, 2009].

The certificate’s contribution is therefore the lower-bound theory, the two-resource map, and the explicitly priced nuisance, not a finite-sample power advantage.

Limitations. (i) Two-axis support: at the registered 41-cell density the CI-separation criterion failed, but it is recovered at higher design density (unanimous strict non-overlap by 635 cells, with the additive form 2.2× better than the nearest alternative), confirming the registered sample-limited reading. The per-axis exponent-containment sub-test remains the finer residual check (Appendix G.9). (ii) Contour constants do not transfer across shift intensities (rate-shape and ordering only; the drift is systematic and monotone in intensity, Appendix G.9). (iii) Localized-geometry evidence is restricted to

family 1 plus qualified family-2 within-pair structure. (iv) B<sup>′</sup> validity is conditional on the pre-registered shift model and off-partition robustness is not claimed: the real workload shows refusal-status invariance only, and the synthetic breakage sweep above (Appendix G.9) is a sensitivity characterization, not a guarantee. (v) The real-workload scope is a single-corpus domain-shift audit with no positive certification, with the post-hoc evaluation-set frontier estimate below the floor across the whole tested operating plane

, both legs; per-α bootstrap, not a population proof). (vi) The implementable certificate is far more sample-hungry than oracle weights: those practical constants (reported in full above) are harsh but fully characterized, one slice of an envelope rather than an isolated point (Appendix G.9).

A hard coverage floor is a statistical object in its own right: it makes the feasibility frontier operational, splits certification cost, in the model-split sense of Theorem 1, into labeled-source and unlabeled-target resources, and surfaces a localized accepted-region functional (not global ESS) that drives the upper-bound variance proxy and organizes the lower-bound hard-slice geometry. This correspondence rests on the matched bound structure and the family-1 experiments, and a fixed ESS separation theorem is left open. Certification with honest refusal is implementable under a pre-registered stratifiedshift model: the formal-guarantee arms are valid by theorem, with 0 violations across the 591 cells they certify on the synthetic grid; on the real workload its output is honest refusal (2,000/2,000), a feasibility verdict, not validity evidence.

Outlook. The pre-registered empirical program (Appendix G.10) is largely complete, and two directions remain. First, beyond the clean B<sup>′</sup> family-1 evidence, the localized-geometry comparison on family 2 remains censored; an uncensored family-2 rerun with a fixed-range-constant oracle test would test whether the localized accepted-region functional governs the rate beyond B<sup>′</sup> family 1. Second, the nuisance theory is settled only on one side: the K-free necessary core is proved for lattice-valued certification in the known-η submodel, and no lower bound forces a separate source-covariate split for estimating p at the population level (Theorem 8); whether unknown-η Model-B<sup>′</sup> admits a K-free certificate, or instead forces K back through the unknown-η source↔target alignment, is the central open edge.

paragraph_content.content: Table 1 compresses a line-by-line analysis of whether each nearest verified prior line yields, by direct adaptation, any of the paper’s five objects: the hard floor as afinite-sample certified object under covariate shift, β-indexed lower bounds, the two-resource
map, the localized accepted-region functional, and the nuisance-priced implementable upper bound. This appendix expands each row.

SCoRE [Bai and Jin, 2026]. SCoRE controls general selection-conditioned risks through weighted e-values, including a covariate-shift treatment with an estimated-weight robustness analysis. Adding a floor test to SCoRE plausibly recovers a U1-style validity statement (this is the concession that opens

, but nothing in the framework produces a lower bound, a feasibility frontier, or rate theory: the robustness analysis prices estimated weights into the e-value, not into a certifiable-slack threshold, and no quantity indexed by
appears. The two-resource split cannot be read off either, because no result separates the labeled and unlabeled sample roles.
LEC [Wang et al., 2025b] and BalanceRAG [Jia et al., 2026]. LEC owns the ratio linearization this paper inherits
; BalanceRAG owns cascaded two-dimensional lattice calibration with multiplicity accounting. Both are exchangeable: no shift, hence no weights, no frontier in
, and no β-indexed statement. BalanceRAG’s α-infeasibility declaration (refusing when no lattice point passes) is an honest-refusal mechanism but not a coverage floor: it certifies nothing about
, and no lower bound accompanies it.

Weighted and marginal conformal risk control under shift [Tibshirani et al., 2019, Zecchin et al., 2025]. This family owns the weight machinery: weighted exchangeability, weighted CRC generalization bounds, and the estimatedweight repair toolkit [Yang et al., 2024, Kato et al., 2023, Wang and Goel, 2026, Laghuvarapu et al., 2026]. The certified estimand is marginal risk or coverage (not the selection-conditioned ratio), and no floor constraint co-exists with the risk statement. The complexity quantities that appear are global ESS-type functionals of w; the localized accepted-region functional cannot be recovered because no accepted set is distinguished by the analysis. No lower bound appears in the cited works of this line (we make no claim about the broader literature).

High-probability risk control under shift [Almeida et al., 2025]. We separate this work from the marginal line above, because its estimand reaches further than that grouping suggests. Theorem 9 gives high-probability control under target covariate shift for a conditional risk
\mathbb { E } _ { Q } [ \breve { L } ( X , Y ; \lambda ) \mid ^ { - } ( X , Y ) \in A ( \lambda ) ]

we certify. So the ratio estimand under shift is within its reach, and we mark that capability present in Table 1. What does not follow is the rest of the map: the risk statement stands alone, with no hard coverage floor certified jointly against it, hence no second resource and no β-indexed lower bound; complexity is not reported through a localized accepted-region functional; and the estimated-weight treatment proceeds under an assumed weight accuracy rather than a finite-sample weight-estimation-error guarantee, so the nuisance is not priced as an explicit increment matched from below. The non-derivability claim for this line is therefore about the floor-indexed map, not about the ratio estimand.

Non-monotone CRC [Aldirawi et al., 2026]. The nearest line in distribution-free lower-bound theory proves a matching minimax lower bound for conformal risk control under non-monotone losses, using a Fano argument over a finite tuning-parameter grid. It is single-axis (excess risk in n) and floor-free; the analysis is extended to distribution shift by importance weighting, but no coverage-floor parameter appears, so there is no frontier, no second resource, and no unlabeled axis. Remark 12 details why neither statement implies the other despite the shared minimax toolkit.

Reject-option classifiers [Franc et al., 2023]; selective QA under shift [Kamath et al., 2020]. The reject-option line poses the floor as a population object: the bounded-abstention model fixes a coverage floor and minimizes selective risk, the bounded-improvement model fixes risk and maximizes coverage, and the optimal strategy is characterized (a Bayes classifier with a randomized selection function). It supplies no finite-sample certificate, no covariate-shift weighting, no β-indexed lower bound, and no labeled/unlabeled resource split; it is the population precedent for the object, not for any of the five finite-sample contributions here. Selective QA under domain shift [Kamath et al., 2020] studies exactly the deployment regime of our real-workload audit (abstain under shift to keep accuracy high), but with a learned calibrator and no validity guarantee or floor certificate, so it motivates the audit rather than competing with its certificate.

Inherited machinery, credited. We inherit and do not claim: weighted e-values and learn-then-test multiplicity [Angelopoulos et al., 2021, Laufer-Goldshtein et al., 2023], cascade multiplicity accounting [Jia et al., 2026], the ratio linearization [Wang et al., 2025b], empirical-Bernstein and betting-based concentration [Maurer and Pontil, 2009, Waudby-Smith and Ramdas, 2024], and the Le Cam two-point technique [Tsybakov, 2009]. What is new is not the floor as a population object (the reject-option line [Franc et al., 2023] already poses guaranteed-coverage selective risk) but the floor as afinite-sample certified object under covariate shift, and everything the floor then creates: the frontier, the β-indexed two-resource map, the localized functional, and the budgeted-nuisance implementable upper bound.
